games.title: Touch Me
games.note: An arcade memory game: repeat a growing sequence of lights and tones.

games.title: Simon
games.dev: Ralph Baer and Howard Morrison (Milton Bradley)
games.note: An electronic memory game launched at Studio 54 in New York: repeat the sequence of four coloured lights.

games.title: Dance Aerobics
games.note: Played on the Power Pad floor mat by copying an instructor's steps; part of Bandai's Family Trainer series in Japan.

games.title: PaRappa the Rapper
games.note: Musician Masaya Matsuura made it with artist Rodney Greenblat; making the characters paper-flat was Matsuura's idea.

games.title: Beatmania
games.note: A DJ game with keys and a turntable; its success led Konami to rename its music division Bemani.

games.title: Pop'n Music
games.note: Nine big colourful buttons replace Beatmania's keys and turntable.

games.title: Dance Dance Revolution
games.note: Played with the feet on a four-arrow dance pad; the only Bemani game to become a big hit outside Japan.

games.title: GuitarFreaks
games.note: Played on a guitar-shaped controller with three fret buttons and a picking lever.

games.title: DrumMania
games.note: An electronic drum kit controller; its cabinets could link with GuitarFreaks for three-player sessions.

games.title: Frequency
games.note: Harmonix's first console game: players switch between instrument tracks on a tunnel of note lanes.

games.title: Amplitude
games.note: Its licensed songs included tracks by Blink-182 and David Bowie.

games.title: Karaoke Revolution
games.note: Published by Konami; it sold four times as many copies as Frequency or Amplitude.

games.title: Rock Band
games.note: Guitar, bass, drums and vocals together in one band; MTV Games owned Harmonix at the time.

games.title: Rock Band 4
games.note: Weekly song downloads continued until January 2024.

games.title: Beat Saber
games.note: Players slice flying blocks to the beat with two sabers in VR; co-founder Jaroslav Beck composed the music.

games.title: Taiko no Tatsujin
games.note: Players beat a full-size taiko drum controller in time to pop songs and anime themes.

games.title: Gitaroo Man
games.note: Its hero played guitar four years before Guitar Hero, using an ordinary controller.

games.title: Osu! Tatakae! Ouendan
games.note: A cheer squad helps people in trouble while players tap circles in time on the touchscreen.

games.title: Elite Beat Agents
games.note: A Western version of Ouendan with secret agents and Western pop songs, made after strong import demand.

games.title: osu!
games.note: A free PC rhythm game by Australian developer Dean Herbert; players make and share the song maps.

games.title: Rhythm Tengoku
games.note: Japan-only; it began as an idea from pop producer Tsunku. The series became Rhythm Heaven in the West.

games.title: Beat Sneak Bandit
games.note: A one-touch stealth game where every move has to land on the beat.

games.title: WarioWare, Inc.: Mega Microgames!
games.note: Over 200 'microgames' lasting a few seconds each; a group of developers first made it in secret.

games.title: Mario Artist: Polygon Studio
games.note: A Japan-only 3D modelling tool for the 64DD disk drive, with a microgame mode called Sound Bomber.

games.title: Crypt of the NecroDancer
games.note: Every move must land on the beat of Danny Baranowsky's soundtrack, and it supports dance mats.

games.title: Just Dance
games.note: It overcame poor reviews to topple Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2's best-seller status.

games.title: Rayman Raving Rabbids
games.note: A minigame collection in which the screaming Rabbids stole the show from Rayman.

games.title: Rayman Raving Rabbids: TV Party
games.note: Billed as the 'first video game you can play with your butt', thanks to the Wii Balance Board.

games.title: Mario Party
games.note: Some minigames had players spin the analog stick with their palms, causing blisters; Nintendo offered protective gloves.

games.title: You Don't Know Jack
games.note: An irreverent trivia game show; its maker Jellyvision later became Jackbox Games.

games.title: The Jackbox Party Pack
games.note: Players answer on their own phones or tablets through a web browser, so no extra controllers are needed.

games.title: EyeToy: Play
games.note: Bundled with the EyeToy USB camera, which put players' own image on screen to swat and wave at targets.

games.title: SingStar
games.note: Came with two USB microphones and scored players' pitch while the original music videos played.

games.title: Samba de Amigo
games.note: Played by shaking a pair of maraca controllers in time to Latin songs.

links.took: Repeat-the-sequence play; Ralph Baer called Touch Me 'nice gameplay, terrible execution'.
links.added: A round handheld toy with four coloured buttons and pleasant musical tones.
links.extra: Baer also called Touch Me 'visually boring' with 'miserable, rasping sounds'.

links.took: Simon popularized watch-and-repeat sequence games.
links.added: Rap lessons: a teacher raps a line, then the player repeats it in rhythm.
links.extra: Rodney Greenblat described an early demo as a 'rap-music-Simon-says-game'.

links.took: Stepping on a floor mat in time with on-screen moves, as Dance Aerobics did on the Power Pad.
links.added: Scrolling arrows timed to dance music, with judged steps in arcade cabinets.
links.extra: No documented influence; shown as an early example of mat-based rhythm play.

links.took: Pressing buttons in time to music, the template PaRappa set for rhythm games.
links.added: A DJ cabinet with keys and a turntable, playing along to club tracks.
links.extra: Wikipedia names Konami's Bemani series among the games that followed PaRappa's template.

links.took: Hitting notes in time to music, following the template PaRappa set.
links.added: A guitar controller, a scrolling note highway and licensed rock songs.

links.took: PaRappa's press-in-time rhythm template, which Wikipedia says later games followed.
links.added: Dancing with the feet on a pad instead of pressing buttons.

links.took: Performing in time to music, following PaRappa's rhythm-game template.
links.added: Copying a dancer's full-body moves with a motion controller.

links.took: PaRappa's rhythm-game template of acting in time to music.
links.added: Maraca controllers shaken high, middle or low to Latin pop songs.

links.took: Konami's Bemani format of notes scrolling toward a timing line.
links.added: Arrows played with the feet on a dance pad.

links.took: Beatmania's falling notes and Bemani arcade format.
links.added: Nine big colourful buttons and a cute cartoon style for a wider audience.

links.took: The Bemani note-scrolling arcade format.
links.added: A guitar-shaped controller with three fret buttons and a picking lever.

links.took: Bemani's instrument-controller format.
links.added: An electronic drum kit; cabinets could link with GuitarFreaks for Session Mode.

links.took: Playing along on a guitar-shaped controller; RedOctane wanted a GuitarFreaks-style game in the West.
links.added: Five fret buttons, star power and Western rock songs.
links.extra: Wikipedia says Guitar Hero was inspired by Bemani's GuitarFreaks.

links.took: Frequency's instrument tracks, played by switching lanes.
links.added: A flatter track layout, licensed hits and online play.

links.took: Harmonix's lanes of notes for each instrument track, first built for Frequency.
links.added: A guitar controller and a single scrolling note highway for one instrument.

links.took: Harmonix's note lanes for instrument tracks, carried over from Frequency and Amplitude.
links.added: A plastic guitar, five frets, star power and a career of rock gigs.

links.took: Harmonix's note-highway guitar play from Guitar Hero.
links.added: Drums, bass and microphone vocals, so a full band plays together.
links.extra: Activision kept Guitar Hero after buying RedOctane; Harmonix made Rock Band under MTV.

links.took: Bemani's instrument games, which Wikipedia says led to Guitar Hero and Rock Band.
links.added: A whole band of plastic instruments playing one song together.

links.took: DrumMania's drum kit controller, a concept Wikipedia says Harmonix later appropriated.
links.added: Drums as one part of a four-person band.

links.took: Harmonix's singing and pitch-detection work from Karaoke Revolution.
links.added: Vocals as one part of a full band, alongside guitar, bass and drums.

links.took: Rock Band's four-person band play and song library.
links.added: Freestyle guitar solos, and support for older instruments and downloaded songs.
links.extra: Rock Band 2 and 3 came in between.

links.took: Guitar Hero popularized note highways that send notes toward the player in time to music.
links.added: Swinging two VR sabers in set directions to slice blocks, and dodging walls.

links.took: Arcade rhythm success: Namco moved into the genre after the hits of Beatmania and Dance Dance Revolution.
links.added: A taiko drum controller hit on its face and rim, with pop and anime songs.
links.extra: Namco first planned a guitar-based rhythm game, which was cancelled.

links.took: Proof that rhythm games could be arcade hits, which Namco followed after DDR and Beatmania.
links.added: Drumming instead of dancing, with a big taiko drum and two sticks.

links.took: Creator Keiichi Yano's rhythm-game experience from Gitaroo Man.
links.added: Touchscreen tapping and a cheer squad rescuing ordinary people.

links.took: Ouendan's touchscreen rhythm play and rescue stories.
links.added: Secret agents and Western pop songs for an international audience.
links.extra: Made after strong import demand for the Japanese original.

links.took: Ouendan's core gameplay of tapping circles in time to music.
links.added: A free PC game where fans make and share the song maps, plus extra modes.

links.took: Elite Beat Agents' tap-in-time circles, named with Ouendan as osu!'s core inspiration.
links.added: Mouse or graphics-tablet play on PC, with online rankings.

links.took: Taiko no Tatsujin's drum-hit notes, used in the osu!taiko mode.
links.added: Taiko-style play as one mode in a free, fan-driven PC game.

links.took: Sound Bomber's rapid microgames: Goro Abe said 'This is where the idea for WarioWare came from'.
links.added: Over 200 microgames in a full game, hosted by Wario and his friends.

src.t: Wikipedia: Mario Artist: Polygon Studio (quotes Goro Abe)

links.extra: Programmer Kouichi Kawamoto came up with the Sound Bomber concept.

links.took: Short, quirky minigames from the WarioWare developer; Wikipedia notes clear parallels.
links.added: Tsunku's music and games played by listening to the rhythm, not watching cues.

links.took: Designer Simon Flesser cites Rhythm Tengoku's art design and its mix of beats and back beats.
links.added: One-touch stealth: sneaking past guards to steal back clocks, always on the beat.

links.took: Rayman himself and Ubisoft's platformer series.
links.added: A minigame party collection where the screaming Rabbids stole the show.

links.took: The Rabbids' minigame party format.
links.added: A TV-channel theme, Balance Board games and a dance minigame reworked around poses.

links.took: A pose-based dance minigame from the Rabbids series, which became Just Dance's concept.
links.added: Copying an on-screen dancer to real pop songs with a Wii Remote.
links.extra: Just Dance was made by a team of about 20 at Ubisoft Paris.

links.took: The dance game, reversed: Gregoire Spillmann said older dance games had players press buttons with their feet.
links.added: Copying a dancer's moves with a motion controller, with no mat or arrows.

links.took: Hard but fair roguelike design; Ryan Clark admired how Spelunky gives players control over their fate.
links.added: Turn-based moves that must land on the music's beat.

src.t: Wikipedia: Crypt of the NecroDancer (cites Ryan Clark, Mashable)

links.took: Turn-based, procedurally generated dungeons; Clark set out to keep roguelike turns.
links.added: Turns tied to the soundtrack's beat, leaving no time to stop and think.

links.took: DDR popularized stepping in time to the beat; NecroDancer even supports dance mats.
links.added: Dungeon crawling and combat where every move must match the beat.

links.took: Mario and his cast, in a spin-off.
links.added: A digital board game with four-player minigames, made by Hudson Soft.

links.took: Jellyvision's irreverent party trivia; the company later became Jackbox Games.
links.added: Phones as controllers and a bundle of party games, including Fibbage and Drawful.
links.extra: The first pack included an updated You Don't Know Jack.

links.took: SCE London Studio's party games for PlayStation 2 add-ons, after EyeToy: Play.
links.added: USB microphones, pitch scoring and real music videos.

links.took: EyeToy popularized camera-based party games where players move their bodies.
links.added: Full-body depth tracking for sports like football, bowling and track and field.

links.took: EyeToy popularized party games played by moving your body.
links.added: A motion-sensing remote swung like a racket, bat or bowling ball.
